title: Reading Between the Lines: Survey Reports
text:
Many newspapers now publish reports based on large surveys rather than on the opinions of single experts. Researchers say this approach gives readers a clearer picture of public attitudes, because it draws on the answers of thousands of people. However, the results are only as reliable as the questions that were asked. A poorly worded question can produce misleading figures, so careful readers should always check how the survey was conducted.

When you read an article of this kind, it is useful to look for the sample size and the date of the survey. A report that describes a small group of respondents collected several months ago may not reflect current opinion. Writers also tend to highlight the most surprising finding in the headline, so the main body of the text can tell a more balanced story. Taking a few minutes to read the full report will help you judge the evidence for yourself.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what does a survey based on thousands of people give readers?
options: Results that are always completely accurate
A clearer picture of public attitudes
A cheaper alternative to expert opinion
Only the views of professional researchers

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what should a reader look for when reading an article about a survey?
options: The name of the newspaper editor
The number of photographs in the article
The sample size and the date of the survey

questions.text: What does the writer imply about the headlines of survey articles?
options: They always give the complete and balanced story.
They may emphasize the most surprising result rather than the full picture.
They are written by the researchers who carried out the survey.
They are usually much shorter than the main text.

questions.text: What can the reader infer from the phrase 'only as reliable as the questions that were asked'?
options: Surveys should never be published in newspapers.
The quality of a survey depends heavily on how its questions are designed.
Experts always write better questions than journalists.
Longer surveys are always more reliable than shorter ones.

vocabulary.definition: a study that collects information by asking many people questions
able to be trusted to give correct results
giving a wrong idea about something
people who answer the questions in a survey
giving fair attention to different sides of a topic

paragraph_translations: Багато газет тепер публікують звіти, які базуються на великих опитуваннях, а не на думках окремих експертів. Дослідники кажуть, що такий підхід дає читачам чіткішу картину громадської думки, адже він спирається на відповіді тисяч людей. Проте результати є настільки надійними, наскільки надійними є запитання, які ставилися. Погано сформульоване запитання може дати оманливі цифри, тому уважні читачі завжди мають перевіряти, як проводилося опитування.

Читаючи статтю такого типу, корисно звернути увагу на розмір вибірки та дату опитування. Звіт, який описує невелику групу респондентів, зібраних кілька місяців тому, може не відображати поточної думки. Автори також схильні виділяти в заголовку найнесподіваніший результат, тому основний текст може розповідати більш збалансовану історію. Кілька хвилин на читання повного звіту допоможуть вам самостійно оцінити докази.
